title: "JMeter: Load Testing Basics"
description: "A worked lesson based on the supplied Spring Cloud course."

**Course source:** Day 2 §4.1. **Running example:** a shop with Product, Order and User services.

## A successful request is not a capacity test

The shop works when one customer places an order. What happens at 100 requests/s? The course uses **Apache JMeter** to exercise services and investigate overload.

Define a test journey before generating traffic:

~~~text
GET product 7 -> GET user 9 -> POST order
~~~

Each request should have success checks. Without assertions, a test that receives thousands of 503 responses may appear to have produced high throughput even though the business function failed.

## Model demand carefully

**Virtual users** approximate concurrent actors, while **arrival rate** states how many requests begin per second. Those are not interchangeable when response time changes. Use realistic think time, response sizes and a gradual ramp.

Record p50/p95/p99 latency, requests per second, failure rate, active connections and saturation of downstream dependencies. Averages conceal long-tail delays that customers feel.

## Baseline, stress and endurance

**Baseline:** verify one normal flow and establish latency. **Load:** run at expected volume. **Stress:** increase above target to find the limiting resource. **Endurance:** sustain realistic load long enough to expose leaks and backlog growth.

Test against a controlled environment with representative data; never direct uncoordinated high-volume tests at a production site.

## Interpret the results

If p95 latency rises while Product CPU is low, suspect waiting on a connection pool, database lock, DNS or network. CPU alone does not identify the bottleneck.

The teaching lab is single-process and stores orders in memory; it is suitable for learning endpoints, not for deriving production throughput numbers.

[Apache JMeter documentation](https://jmeter.apache.org/usermanual/).

## Questions to answer aloud

What problem does this design solve? Which guarantee does it give, and which guarantee does it **not** give? How would you detect incorrect operation?
